10.deck: A curious child tests the rules of a world that keeps changing around her.
overview: Wonderland’s rules sound authoritative, but rarely stay consistent.
Alice’s confidence grows when she questions what others take for granted.
takeaways: Identity can survive change.
Authority deserves scrutiny when it cannot explain itself.
Language can clarify or confuse depending on who controls it.

sections.label: Chapter I: Down the Rabbit-Hole
sections.title: Down the Rabbit-Hole
sections.summary:
Alice is bored beside her sister when a White Rabbit hurries past, consulting a pocket watch. She follows it down a deep rabbit hole and reaches a hall of locked doors. A tiny key opens a door to a lovely garden, but Alice is too large to pass through. A drink makes her small and a cake makes her grow again. These sudden changes establish the dreamlike rules of Wonderland.

She soon learns that reaching the garden will take more than finding the right door. When she changes size, she leaves the key out of reach, and every solution seems to create a new obstacle. The opening makes her curiosity feel adventurous and unsettling at once.

sections.label: Chapter II: The Pool of Tears
sections.title: The Pool of Tears
sections.summary:
Alice grows so tall that she can scarcely see her feet and cries until a pool forms around her. After the White Rabbit drops his fan and gloves, she shrinks again and slips into the pool. There she meets a Mouse and other animals swept up by her tears. Alice tries to make conversation, but her talk of cats and dogs alarms the Mouse.

As she swims, Alice tries to decide whether she is still the same person she was at home. She attempts polite conversation with the Mouse, but her familiar examples are exactly what its companions fear. Wonderland makes ordinary manners unreliable.

sections.label: Chapter III: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
sections.title: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
sections.summary:
The wet animals gather on shore. The Dodo proposes a Caucus-race with no clear start or finish; everyone is declared a winner, and Alice supplies the prizes. The Mouse begins a story about why it dislikes cats and dogs. Alice mistakes its long tale for its tail and loses track of the story. Her mention of her cat Dinah drives the company away.

Alice gives the others comfits as prizes and is awarded a thimble from her own pocket. The ceremony is funny because everyone treats it with solemn importance despite its empty rules. Her efforts to ask about the Mouse’s story only create more confusion.

sections.label: Chapter IV: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
sections.title: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
sections.summary:
The White Rabbit mistakes Alice for his servant Mary Ann and sends her to fetch his gloves. Inside his house, Alice drinks from another bottle and grows until she fills the room. The Rabbit and his helpers try to remove her; Bill the lizard is sent down the chimney. Small cakes thrown into the house make Alice shrink, and she escapes into the woods, where a huge puppy briefly blocks her path.

Trapped in the Rabbit’s house, Alice can hear the animals planning ways to force her out, though none understands her predicament. Her escape leaves her searching for a way to control her size rather than simply reacting to each drink or cake.

sections.label: Chapter V: Advice from a Caterpillar
sections.title: Advice from a Caterpillar
sections.summary:
A Caterpillar asks Alice who she is, a question she finds difficult after changing size so often. He advises her that opposite sides of a mushroom will make her grow or shrink. Alice experiments, briefly stretching her neck high above the trees, where a Pigeon calls her a serpent. By carefully balancing the mushroom pieces, she returns to a manageable size and approaches a little house.

The Caterpillar is calm where Alice is frustrated, and his questions make her struggle to describe herself. His advice is practical but incomplete: she has to test the mushroom pieces herself and learn how to balance their effects.

sections.label: Chapter VI: Pig and Pepper
sections.title: Pig and Pepper
sections.summary:
At the Duchess’s house, pepper fills the kitchen and the cook throws dishes. Alice takes the Duchess’s baby outside, only to see it turn into a pig. The Cheshire Cat appears and directs her toward the March Hare or the Hatter, warning that both are mad. Its vanishing grin leaves Alice to choose her next encounter.

The Duchess treats the chaos in her kitchen as normal. Alice’s attempt to rescue the baby ends in a transformation she cannot prevent, while the Cheshire Cat’s shifting appearance makes even a helpful conversation feel uncertain.

sections.label: Chapter VII: A Mad Tea-Party
sections.title: A Mad Tea-Party
sections.summary:
Alice joins the Hatter, March Hare, and sleepy Dormouse at a table where it is always tea time. Their riddles, wordplay, and quarrels about Time make ordinary conversation impossible. The Dormouse tells a strange story about three sisters in a treacle well. Frustrated, Alice leaves, finds a door in a tree, and finally reaches the garden she has sought since arriving.

The Hatter asks a riddle with no answer and claims that Time has stopped for him at six o’clock. The company keeps changing places instead of washing the cups. Alice eventually recognizes that staying at the table will not make the conversation clearer.

sections.label: Chapter VIII: The Queen’s Croquet-Ground
sections.title: The Queen’s Croquet-Ground
sections.summary:
Alice finds gardeners painting white roses red to avoid the Queen of Hearts’ anger. The Queen arrives and repeatedly orders executions, but Alice resists being intimidated. Croquet is played with flamingoes as mallets, hedgehogs as balls, and soldiers as hoops, so the game has almost no stable rules. The Cheshire Cat’s floating head causes another dispute before the Queen sends Alice to the Mock Turtle.

The gardeners and soldiers obey the Queen’s threats, yet her orders rarely lead to actual executions. Alice notices the gap between the Queen’s frightening language and what really happens, even as the game becomes more impossible to play.

sections.label: Chapter IX: The Mock Turtle’s Story
sections.title: The Mock Turtle’s Story
sections.summary:
The Duchess briefly accompanies Alice and draws a moral from almost everything she says. The Queen then sends Alice with the Gryphon to meet the Mock Turtle. In a melancholy account of his school under the sea, the Mock Turtle describes subjects whose names are absurd twists on ordinary lessons. Alice listens, puzzled by the mixture of sorrow and nonsense.

The Duchess’s constant search for morals briefly turns every remark into a lesson. The Mock Turtle’s account of school makes lessons sound familiar and absurd at the same time, leaving Alice unsure whether to ask questions or simply listen.

sections.label: Chapter X: The Lobster Quadrille
sections.title: The Lobster Quadrille
sections.summary:
The Mock Turtle and Gryphon describe and demonstrate the Lobster Quadrille, a dance in which sea creatures throw lobsters out to sea. Their songs and explanations keep turning familiar words into jokes and contradictions. Alice tries to tell them about her own adventures, but her recitations come out wrong. A call to the trial interrupts their conversation, and the Gryphon leads Alice away.

The Gryphon and Mock Turtle insist on the dance’s rules while describing a world Alice has never seen. Their songs and Alice’s failed recitations show how words can slip out of her control before the trial pulls her into a more threatening kind of nonsense.

sections.label: Chapter XI: Who Stole the Tarts?
sections.title: Who Stole the Tarts?
sections.summary:
The Knave of Hearts is on trial for stealing the Queen’s tarts. Alice watches a disorderly court in which jurors write down trivial details and the King struggles to manage witnesses. The Hatter’s nervous testimony and the cook’s unhelpful answers provide little evidence. As the proceedings continue, Alice begins to grow again and becomes less willing to accept the court’s authority.

The jurors write down names and minor details as though paperwork could make the proceedings fair. The King and Queen treat witnesses as obstacles to a verdict they already want. Alice’s growing body matches her growing willingness to object.

sections.label: Chapter XII: Alice’s Evidence
sections.title: Alice’s Evidence
sections.summary:
Called as a witness, Alice accidentally upsets the jury box. The King invents a rule to remove anyone taller than a mile, while an unsigned poem is treated as evidence even though nobody can explain it. Alice openly rejects the trial’s nonsense and calls the court a pack of cards. The cards fly at her, and she wakes beside her sister, realizing that Wonderland was a dream.

Alice’s sister listens as she wakes and imagines that Alice will remember the dream long after childhood. The story ends in an ordinary setting, but it leaves open the possibility that imagination and curiosity can remain part of Alice’s life.

23.deck: A miser is shown his past, the lives around him, and the future his choices may create.
overview: The ghosts give Scrooge evidence, but he must choose what to do with it.
Dickens links private kindness to responsibility for other people.
takeaways: Regret matters when it changes action.
Generosity is a habit, not a holiday performance.
The future is a warning rather than a fixed verdict.

sections.label: Stave I: Marley’s Ghost
sections.title: Marley’s Ghost
sections.summary:
Ebenezer Scrooge rejects his nephew Fred’s Christmas invitation and refuses a request to help the poor. He grudgingly gives his clerk Bob Cratchit Christmas Day off. At home, the ghost of his former partner Jacob Marley appears, burdened by a chain forged from his selfish acts. Marley warns Scrooge that he is making a heavier chain for himself. Three spirits will visit, giving him a chance to change before his life is over.

Scrooge calls the prisons and workhouses sufficient help for the poor, making clear how little he sees the people around him. Marley’s ghost says that caring for others should have been his true business. The coming visits offer Scrooge a chance to see what his habits have cost.

sections.label: Stave II: The First of the Three Spirits
sections.title: The First of the Three Spirits
sections.summary:
The Ghost of Christmas Past takes Scrooge through scenes from his own life. He sees his lonely childhood at school, his sister Fan’s affection, and a joyful party held by his generous employer Fezziwig. The spirit then shows how Scrooge’s fixation on wealth ended his engagement to Belle. A later glimpse of Belle’s family makes clear what a different life he might have had. Scrooge cannot bear more and forces the spirit’s light out of sight.

The spirit shows Scrooge his lonely school days, the joy of his sister Fan, and the warmth of a party given by his employer Fezziwig. He also watches Belle end their engagement when money becomes his ruling interest. Seeing Belle’s later family makes that loss painfully concrete.

sections.label: Stave III: The Second of the Three Spirits
sections.title: The Second of the Three Spirits
sections.summary:
The Ghost of Christmas Present shows Scrooge celebrations throughout the city and beyond. At the Cratchits’ modest dinner, the family is loving despite hardship, and Scrooge learns that Tiny Tim may die if nothing changes. He also sees Fred’s gathering, where people laugh at Scrooge but still wish him well. Near the end, the spirit reveals two neglected children called Ignorance and Want, exposing the human cost of the indifference Scrooge has defended.

The spirit also takes Scrooge beyond familiar homes, showing people at sea and in remote places keeping Christmas together. At the end of the night, two neglected children called Ignorance and Want appear beneath its robe. Their presence turns the visit from comfort toward warning.

sections.label: Stave IV: The Last of the Spirits
sections.title: The Last of the Spirits
sections.summary:
The silent Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows strangers discussing an unnamed man’s death without grief. Scrooge sees thieves selling the dead man’s possessions and the Cratchits mourning Tiny Tim. He finally discovers that the unmourned man is himself. At his own grave, Scrooge begs for a chance to alter the future. The vision is a warning of what his present choices may bring, not a fate he must accept.

Scrooge sees businessmen discuss a death without grief and thieves sell the dead man’s belongings. In the Cratchit home, he sees sorrow over Tiny Tim; at a grave, he discovers that the lonely dead man is himself. He asks whether these shadows can still be changed.

sections.label: Stave V: The End of It
sections.title: The End of It
sections.summary:
Scrooge wakes on Christmas morning, delighted that he still has time to act. He sends a large turkey to the Cratchits, gives generously to charity, and joins Fred for dinner. The next day he raises Bob’s salary and offers help to the family. Dickens closes by describing a lasting change: Scrooge becomes a kinder employer, neighbor, and friend, and Tiny Tim lives.

Scrooge also surprises a charity collector with a generous gift and makes peace with Fred’s household. His promise to Bob extends beyond one festive morning: he plans to support the family and carry the day’s lessons into the rest of his life.

16.deck: A man builds an extravagant life to win back a past that cannot be restored.
overview: Nick Carraway moves to Long Island and becomes the witness to Jay Gatsby’s pursuit of Daisy Buchanan.
The novel places wealth, class, and spectacle beside the emotional cost of trying to remake an earlier love.
takeaways: Money can stage an image, but cannot make another person live inside it.
Nick’s shifting judgment is part of the story.
The green light begins as a private hope and ends as a wider symbol of unreachable futures.

sections.label: Chapter I
sections.title: The green light
sections.summary:
Nick settles in West Egg and visits his cousin Daisy and her husband Tom across the bay. Their elegant home cannot conceal Tom’s affair or Daisy’s unease. Back home, Nick sees his mysterious neighbor Gatsby reaching toward a green light on Daisy’s dock.

At dinner, Tom praises a book about racial hierarchy while Jordan Baker moves casually through the Buchanans’ polished social world. A phone call from Tom’s lover interrupts the evening. Nick’s first impression of privilege is therefore mixed with dishonesty and restlessness.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: The valley of ashes
sections.summary:
Tom takes Nick through the industrial wasteland between Long Island and Manhattan and introduces Myrtle Wilson, his mistress. Their apartment party grows loud and cruel; when Myrtle repeatedly says Daisy’s name, Tom strikes her and breaks her nose.

Myrtle’s husband George runs a garage in the valley of ashes and does not know the full truth of her relationship with Tom. In New York, Myrtle takes on an air of superiority as guests gather around her. The violence at the party exposes how little protection Tom’s attention gives her.

sections.label: Chapter III
sections.title: Inside Gatsby’s party
sections.summary:
Nick attends one of Gatsby’s lavish parties, where guests trade rumors without knowing their host. Gatsby proves unexpectedly courteous and reserved. Nick also begins seeing Jordan Baker, while observing how easily gossip replaces knowledge.

Nick first speaks with Gatsby without realizing who he is, a reversal of the party’s endless gossip. A guest examines Gatsby’s surprisingly real library, while a car accident outside ends the night in confusion. Nick leaves with more questions than answers about his host.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: The hidden connection
sections.summary:
Gatsby gives Nick a polished account of his past and introduces him to Meyer Wolfsheim. Jordan then explains the history: Gatsby and Daisy loved each other before the war, and Gatsby has bought his house across the bay to be near her. He asks Nick to arrange a reunion.

Gatsby offers apparent proof of his education and war service, but his rehearsed story does not settle Nick’s doubts. Wolfsheim is linked to the fixing of the 1919 World Series. Jordan’s account of Daisy finally gives Nick a reason for Gatsby’s elaborate life on West Egg.

sections.label: Chapter V
sections.title: Tea with Daisy
sections.summary:
Nick invites Daisy to tea. Gatsby arrives nervous, and their first minutes together are awkward. At Gatsby’s mansion, the two grow close again, but Nick senses that the real Daisy may never match the dream Gatsby has built around her.

Gatsby nearly upsets a clock during the tense reunion, and the rain outside gradually clears as the mood changes. He shows Daisy his rooms and expensive shirts, trying to make visible all he has built since losing her. Nick notices the gap between this display and Gatsby’s private longing.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: James Gatz
sections.summary:
Nick recounts Gatsby’s beginnings as James Gatz and his self-reinvention after meeting Dan Cody. Tom becomes suspicious when he and Daisy attend a Gatsby party. Gatsby wants Daisy to declare she never loved Tom, insisting the past can be repeated.

Gatsby’s account of his youth reveals an early determination to invent a grander self. Daisy does not enjoy his party as he hoped, and Tom’s contempt makes the old class divide plain. Gatsby still imagines that one clear declaration from Daisy could erase the intervening years.

sections.label: Chapter VII
sections.title: The confrontation
sections.summary:
Gatsby ends his parties and replaces his staff as his affair with Daisy deepens. In a hot Manhattan hotel room, Gatsby demands that Daisy reject her marriage, but she cannot give him the absolute answer he wants. Driving home, Daisy strikes and kills Myrtle in Gatsby’s car; Gatsby resolves to take the blame.

Tom questions Gatsby’s business and draws attention to the difference between new money and inherited status. Daisy briefly considers leaving but cannot say she never loved Tom. Myrtle runs toward Gatsby’s car believing Tom is inside; afterward Gatsby waits outside Daisy’s house to protect her, unaware that she has already retreated toward Tom.

sections.label: Chapter VIII
sections.title: The pool
sections.summary:
Gatsby tells Nick more about his courtship of Daisy and continues to wait for her call. George Wilson, grieving Myrtle and misled about the car, arrives at Gatsby’s house, shoots him, and then kills himself. Gatsby dies still attached to a future Daisy will not share.

Nick urges Gatsby to go away, but Gatsby remains fixed on Daisy. Before leaving, Nick tells him he is worth more than the careless people surrounding him. Wilson traces the fatal car to Gatsby and takes revenge on the wrong person, while Daisy remains absent.

sections.label: Chapter IX
sections.title: After the party
sections.summary:
Nick struggles to find mourners for Gatsby’s funeral; the crowds who enjoyed his hospitality vanish. He breaks with Jordan, confronts Tom, and decides to leave the East. Looking across the bay, he reflects on Gatsby’s hope and the human effort to move forward while being pulled toward the past.

Gatsby’s father arrives with evidence of his son’s youthful plans, but almost none of the party guests come to the funeral. Nick learns how Tom directed Wilson toward Gatsby and sees the Buchanans leave the damage behind. His final reflection widens Gatsby’s longing into a story about hope and the pull of the past.

29.deck: A lawyer follows a trail of violence toward a secret his friend cannot contain.
overview: Gabriel Utterson investigates the disturbing connection between respectable Dr. Jekyll and the violent Edward Hyde.
The mystery gradually turns into an account of how Jekyll tried to divide his public virtue from his hidden desires.
takeaways: A divided identity does not remove responsibility for either half.
The story withholds its explanation until witness accounts and Jekyll’s confession converge.
Reputation can conceal harm as readily as it can reward virtue.

sections.label: Chapter 1
sections.title: Story of the Door
sections.summary:
On a Sunday walk, Enfield tells Utterson how a small, repellent man trampled a child and paid compensation with a cheque signed by the respected Dr. Jekyll. The man, Hyde, also has access to a strange door linked to Jekyll’s home.

Enfield describes how Hyde calmly trampled a young girl in the street and agreed to pay to avoid a scandal. The cheque seemed genuine, making Jekyll’s connection to Hyde hard to dismiss. Utterson chooses discretion, but he cannot forget the door.

sections.label: Chapter 2
sections.title: Search for Mr. Hyde
sections.summary:
Troubled by Jekyll’s will, which leaves his estate to Hyde, Utterson watches the door and finally meets Hyde. His instinctive revulsion deepens his fear that Hyde is blackmailing Jekyll, but Jekyll’s servants say Hyde is allowed into the house.

Utterson also consults Dr. Lanyon, who has fallen out with Jekyll over his scientific ideas. After meeting Hyde, Utterson fears that the man could use Jekyll’s strange will to gain everything. His concern for his friend drives an investigation built from incomplete clues.

sections.label: Chapter 3
sections.title: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
sections.summary:
After a dinner, Utterson presses Jekyll about Hyde. Jekyll insists he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses and asks his friend to protect Hyde’s rights if Jekyll disappears. Utterson promises, though he remains unconvinced.

Jekyll’s request for fairness toward Hyde is unusually urgent. He offers no account of why he feels responsible for this man, leaving Utterson to imagine blackmail or shame. The conversation ends with a promise, not an explanation.

sections.label: Chapter 4
sections.title: The Carew Murder Case
sections.summary:
A maid witnesses Hyde murder Sir Danvers Carew with a cane. Utterson identifies part of the weapon as one he gave Jekyll, and police search Hyde’s rooms. Hyde has vanished, leaving evidence but no clear account of his relationship with Jekyll.

The victim’s identity makes the crime impossible to treat as a private scandal. Police find signs of Hyde’s hurried departure, yet his history is difficult to trace. Utterson is left holding a piece of the cane and a stronger suspicion that Jekyll is hiding something grave.

sections.label: Chapter 5
sections.title: Incident of the Letter
sections.summary:
Jekyll shows Utterson a letter supposedly written by Hyde, promising not to trouble him again. Utterson’s clerk notices that the letter and Jekyll’s own writing look alike, though the slant differs. Utterson fears his friend has forged evidence to protect a murderer.

Jekyll claims the letter was delivered to him, but the servants know of no messenger. When Utterson’s clerk compares the handwriting, the resemblance shakes the lawyer’s faith in his friend. He locks the letter away rather than make his suspicion public.

sections.label: Chapter 6
sections.title: Incident of Dr. Lanyon
sections.summary:
Hyde disappears and Jekyll briefly returns to social life, then shuts himself away. Dr. Lanyon, visibly shaken by something Jekyll has done, refuses to speak of him and dies soon after. He leaves Utterson a sealed account to read only after Jekyll’s death or disappearance.

Lanyon’s sudden decline follows an encounter he refuses to describe. Jekyll’s own doors close just as his old friendships seemed restored. The sealed narrative in Lanyon’s papers ensures that Utterson will eventually hear an explanation, but only after further loss.

sections.label: Chapter 7
sections.title: Incident at the Window
sections.summary:
Utterson and Enfield speak to Jekyll through his window. For a moment he seems willing to join them; then a look of terror crosses his face and he slams the window shut. The two men leave horrified.

The short encounter gives Utterson and Enfield no new facts. Jekyll’s abrupt fear is enough to convince them that something inside the house has changed. Their silent departure captures the limits of an investigation conducted from the street.

sections.label: Chapter 8
sections.title: The Last Night
sections.summary:
Jekyll’s butler Poole asks Utterson for help: a changed voice has been issuing orders from the locked laboratory. They break down the door and find Hyde dead in Jekyll’s clothes. Jekyll is absent, but he has left documents for Utterson.

Poole says the person behind the laboratory door keeps demanding a particular chemical and rejecting each supply. The servants fear that Jekyll has been replaced. Breaking in ends the immediate danger but deepens the mystery, because Hyde’s body and Jekyll’s papers are all that remain.

sections.label: Chapter 9
sections.title: Dr. Lanyon’s Narrative
sections.summary:
Lanyon describes collecting chemicals for Jekyll and receiving a visitor who drinks the mixture before his eyes. Hyde transforms into Jekyll. The sight shatters Lanyon’s understanding of the world and explains why he could no longer face his former friend.

Jekyll’s instructions had brought Lanyon to his house with a drawer of chemicals, then sent Hyde to collect them. Lanyon watches the visitor drink the mixture and change into the friend he once knew. The revelation destroys the ordinary medical explanation Lanyon expected.

sections.label: Chapter 10
sections.title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement
sections.summary:
Jekyll confesses that his potion gave separate form to impulses he had long hidden. He first enjoyed escaping his reputation as Hyde, then found that transformation came without the drug and that the supply he needed could not be replaced. His attempt to divide good and evil made him less able to choose either.

Jekyll explains that Hyde first gave him freedom from the social consequences of his actions. Over time Hyde grew stronger, and Jekyll began changing without choosing to. A later batch of the drug failed because the original chemical had contained an unknown impurity; unable to restore it, Jekyll faced being trapped as Hyde.

28.deck: Two invented identities make courtship easy until everyone demands the truth.
overview: Jack calls himself Ernest in London; Algernon invents an invalid friend to escape social duties.
Their deceptions become a comedy about names, marriage, class, and the performance of respectability.
takeaways: A social label can matter more to these characters than the person behind it.
The play’s paradoxes expose the rules its characters claim to respect.
Its ending resolves the plot by making an absurd coincidence decisive.

sections.label: Act I
sections.title: The double lives
sections.summary:
In Algernon’s London flat, Jack admits that he is known as Ernest in town but Jack at his country estate. He proposes to Gwendolen, who loves the name Ernest. Lady Bracknell rejects him as a suitor after learning he was found as an infant in a handbag at Victoria Station. Algernon discovers the address of Jack’s young ward Cecily and plans a visit.

Algernon calls his invented friend Bunbury a useful escape from unwanted duties and recognizes Jack’s double life when he finds Cecily’s name in a cigarette case. Gwendolen’s delight in the name Ernest matters more to her than Jack’s account of himself. Lady Bracknell’s questions turn the marriage proposal into an inspection of pedigree and income.

sections.label: Act II
sections.title: Mistaken engagements
sections.summary:
At Jack’s country house, Algernon arrives pretending to be the troublesome brother Ernest. Cecily, already fascinated by stories about him, imagines that they are engaged. Jack arrives in mourning for the brother he claims has died, while Gwendolen appears and also claims to be engaged to Ernest. The women compare notes; the men must admit their real names and each seeks a christening.

Cecily has already written an imaginary history of her romance with the man she believes is Ernest. When Gwendolen arrives, their courteous rivalry turns sharp over tea and cake. Jack and Algernon’s plans to be christened show that neither intends to abandon the deception until the women force the issue.

sections.label: Act III
sections.title: The handbag answer
sections.summary:
Lady Bracknell arrives and approves Cecily’s fortune but Jack refuses consent while she opposes his marriage to Gwendolen. Miss Prism is recognized as the governess who accidentally left a baby in a handbag. Jack learns he is Algernon’s older brother and discovers that his given name really is Ernest. Both couples can marry, and the final joke turns Jack’s long deception into a literal truth.

The revelation of Miss Prism’s mistake supplies Jack with a family history that Lady Bracknell will accept. Discovering the name recorded for him gives the comedy its final twist: he has been telling the truth about being Ernest only by accident. The couples’ happy ending leaves Wilde’s satire of social seriousness in place.

24.deck: A secret loan forces Nora Helmer to examine the marriage she thought she understood.
overview: Nora once borrowed money to save her husband Torvald’s health and forged her father’s signature to get it.
When the lender threatens exposure, Nora discovers that her husband values his reputation more than her sacrifice.
takeaways: Nora’s secret is both an act of care and a response to the limited choices available to her.
The tarantella postpones a reckoning she cannot escape.
The final door closes on a marriage built around roles rather than equal understanding.

sections.label: Act I
sections.title: The hidden debt
sections.summary:
At Christmas, Torvald has received a promotion and Nora seems cheerful about their finances. She privately tells Mrs. Linde that she borrowed money years earlier to fund a trip that saved Torvald’s health. Krogstad, the lender, threatens to reveal the debt and her forged signature unless she helps him keep his job at the bank.

Nora has made secret repayments by saving household money and taking copying work, all while letting Torvald think of her as financially naive. Mrs. Linde’s need for paid work throws Nora’s hidden resourcefulness into relief. Krogstad then reveals that the forged signature could be used against her, turning a past act of care into a present threat.

sections.label: Act II
sections.title: The tarantella
sections.summary:
Torvald refuses Nora’s appeal for Krogstad and sends his dismissal. Krogstad places a letter explaining the forgery in Torvald’s locked letterbox. Nora distracts Torvald with a frenzied rehearsal of the tarantella, hoping to delay his reading it, while fearing that the truth will destroy her home.

Nora asks Torvald to reconsider Krogstad’s dismissal, but he sees the appeal as an affront to his authority. Dr. Rank reveals his love and his approaching death, closing another path Nora had considered for help. Her frantic tarantella rehearsal buys time, but the letter remains waiting in the box.

sections.label: Act III
sections.title: The door
sections.summary:
Mrs. Linde and Krogstad reconcile, but she lets his first letter remain so the Helmers must face the truth. Torvald reacts with anger at the threat to his reputation; only after a second letter returns the bond does he offer forgiveness. Nora rejects his sudden change of tone, says they have never understood each other as equals, and leaves to educate herself.

Before the letter is read, Mrs. Linde decides that honesty is better than another concealment. Torvald’s first response to the forgery is to worry about his standing and forbid Nora to raise the children; his relief at the returned bond does not undo what she has heard. Their final conversation forces both to confront how little they have treated Nora as a full person.

100.deck: A stolen dog learns the rules of the northern trail, then hears a life beyond them calling.
overview: Buck begins as a comfortable California pet and becomes a powerful sled dog in the Klondike.
His bond with John Thornton gives him a reason to stay with people even as the wilderness draws him away.
takeaways: Survival changes Buck through experience rather than a single sudden transformation.
The novel pairs brutality on the trail with a genuine bond between Buck and Thornton.
The final call is a choice of belonging as well as an escape from human ownership.

sections.label: Chapter I
sections.title: Into the Primitive
sections.summary:
Buck lives on Judge Miller’s California estate until the gardener’s helper Manuel sells him. Taken north during the gold rush, he fights his captors and is beaten by a man with a club. Buck learns that human authority can be enforced by force even when he believes himself in the right.

He is sold to Perrault and François, who need strong dogs for the mail trail. His first encounter with snow is bewildering. Everything familiar about his old life—warmth, safety, and the assumption that people will protect him—has been removed.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: The Law of Club and Fang
sections.summary:
Buck’s first days among the sled dogs teach him how quickly weakness can be punished. He sees Curly killed by a pack after she falls in a fight, and he understands that there is no pause for mercy on the trail. Spitz, the lead dog, becomes his particular enemy.

Buck learns to sleep under snow, steal food, and pull in harness. He does not simply become savage; he becomes observant and adaptable. The skills that once served him as a household dog are replaced by habits suited to cold and competition.

sections.label: Chapter III
sections.title: The Dominant Primordial Beast
sections.summary:
As the team travels, Buck and Spitz compete for authority. Buck grows stronger and more calculating, undermining Spitz while waiting for a direct contest. A chase after a snowshoe rabbit brings the rivalry to its end when the two dogs fight before the team.

Buck defeats Spitz and takes his place as the dominant dog. The victory is more than a change in rank: Buck has learned to act with the instincts and patience that the trail rewards. His earlier life has become a distant memory.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: Who Has Won to Mastership
sections.summary:
François first tries to put another dog at the front, but Buck refuses every position except the lead. Once there, he drives the team with speed and discipline. The mail route remains punishing, and the dogs are handed to a new driver after weeks of hard travel.

Dave, a dog who lives for his work in the traces, becomes too sick to continue. Attempts to let him rest only distress him; he is allowed back into harness briefly before he falls behind and is put down. Buck sees how little room the trail gives to a working dog who can no longer pull.

sections.label: Chapter V
sections.title: The Toil of Trace and Trail
sections.summary:
Exhausted dogs pass into the hands of Hal, Charles, and Mercedes, inexperienced travelers who overload the sled, mismanage food, and argue instead of learning from the trail. The team weakens as their journey continues. Buck finally refuses to rise when Hal orders him onward.

John Thornton cuts Buck free as Hal beats him. The others drive onto thawing river ice; it breaks, swallowing them and the team. Buck survives because someone recognizes the danger and refuses to treat his exhaustion as disobedience.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: For the Love of a Man
sections.summary:
With Thornton, Buck recovers and forms a bond unlike the obedience demanded by earlier owners. He protects Thornton in a saloon fight and leaps into dangerous water to save him. Thornton trusts him, and Buck responds with affection as fierce as his strength.

At Dawson, Thornton bets that Buck can pull a sled carrying a thousand pounds. Buck succeeds, earning money that lets Thornton pursue a new expedition. His power now serves a person he loves, even while the forest continues to draw his attention.

sections.label: Chapter VII
sections.title: The Sounding of the Call
sections.summary:
Thornton and his partners search for a lost gold mine while Buck spends longer periods wandering, hunting, and meeting a wolf. He returns because of Thornton, but finds the camp attacked by Yeehat warriors and Thornton dead. Buck drives off the attackers in grief and rage.

With that last human tie broken, Buck joins the wolves. The novel ends by placing him in the wilderness he has been approaching throughout the journey, a figure remembered in stories told by people who fear the valley where he now runs.

101.deck: A journey to the distant future turns a dazzling technological idea into a warning about humanity.
overview: An inventor tells his dinner guests that time can be traveled like a fourth dimension.
His account of the Eloi and Morlocks tests easy assumptions about progress and class.
takeaways: The beautiful surface of the future conceals dependence and danger.
The traveler repeatedly revises his theories as new evidence appears.
The far future gives the story a scale larger than any one society.

sections.label: Chapter I
sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary:
At dinner, the Time Traveller argues that time is a fourth dimension and that movement through it should be possible. His guests question the idea, but he treats their objections as problems of habit rather than proof that he is wrong.

He distinguishes ordinary experience of time from a machine that might direct that experience. The conversation is framed through a skeptical narrator, so the reader hears the theory before any extraordinary event can confirm it.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: The Machine
sections.summary:
The Time Traveller demonstrates a small model to his guests. When he presses its controls, the model disappears, leaving the group to debate whether it has truly moved through time or has been hidden by a trick.

He then shows them a larger machine under construction. His confidence is clear, but the witnesses remain uncertain. The chapter turns an abstract claim into a physical invention without yet asking anyone to accept his later story.

sections.label: Chapter III
sections.title: The Time Traveller Returns
sections.summary:
The narrator and other guests return for another dinner and find their host absent. He arrives late, dirty, injured, and visibly shaken, then insists on washing and eating before he tells them where he has been.

His condition is the first evidence that something beyond a dinner-table demonstration has happened. The guests listen as he begins an account that sounds impossible even to people who saw the model vanish. His account begins only after he has eaten and gathered himself, which makes the dinner guests wait for an explanation.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: Time Travelling
sections.summary:
The Time Traveller describes sitting in the full-size machine and moving forward so fast that days and seasons blur around him. He stops in the year 802,701, near a large white sphinx and strange buildings under a warm sky.

Small, graceful people approach him without fear. He initially reads their delicate appearance as a sign that future humanity has escaped the struggles of his own age, an interpretation the rest of the journey will challenge.

sections.label: Chapter V
sections.title: In the Golden Age
sections.summary:
The traveler joins the Eloi, who live among impressive but decaying buildings. They are friendly and beautiful, yet seem childlike, easily tired, and uninterested in sustained thought or work. He struggles to learn their language.

The apparent ease of their world puzzles him. Abundance seems to have made effort unnecessary, but the ruins and the Eloi’s lack of curiosity suggest that a comfortable surface is not the whole story of the future.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: The Sunset of Mankind
sections.summary:
The traveler begins explaining the Eloi through a theory of human progress: perhaps centuries of safety and wealth removed the need for strength or intelligence. He notices that the landscape has been extensively shaped and that many structures are abandoned.

His account sounds plausible to him, but he admits it is only a first explanation. Wells lets the traveler’s confidence reveal how readily a visitor can make a tidy theory from incomplete evidence.

sections.label: Chapter VII
sections.title: A Sudden Shock
sections.summary:
The Time Machine disappears from the place where the traveler left it. Marks near the white sphinx point toward a hidden doorway, and he fears he may be trapped. He also notices dark underground openings and the Eloi’s unease after sunset.

He rescues an Eloi woman named Weena from drowning; she becomes his companion. His search for the machine now has two pressures: he must understand the hidden world below, and he must keep himself and Weena safe at night.

sections.label: Chapter VIII
sections.title: Explanation
sections.summary:
The traveler encounters pale, light-sensitive Morlocks and realizes that the future has two human descendants. He revises his theory: the Eloi may descend from a leisure class, while the Morlocks, who maintain machinery underground, descend from workers.

The apparent paradise depends on labor that its surface dwellers scarcely notice. The traveler’s sympathy for Weena grows, but his discovery also makes him fear that the relationship between the two groups is darker than a simple division of work.

sections.label: Chapter IX
sections.title: The Morlocks
sections.summary:
The traveler descends into a shaft to learn what the Morlocks do beneath the ground. In the darkness he sees machines and faces that unsettle him. They crowd toward him, and his supply of matches becomes a fragile defense.

He escapes back into daylight and begins to suspect that the Morlocks prey upon the Eloi. His expedition has replaced wonder with urgency: recovering the machine will require confronting those who control the hidden spaces around it.

sections.label: Chapter X
sections.title: When Night Came
sections.summary:
Knowing the Morlocks are more dangerous after dark, the traveler plans a route with Weena toward a distant building he hopes will offer supplies. Their journey exposes how vulnerable she is outside the familiar world of the Eloi.

He hopes to find fire, tools, and a place where they can rest before returning to the sphinx. His practical plans are repeatedly shaped by his fear of darkness and by his determination to bring Weena home with him.

sections.label: Chapter XI
sections.title: The Palace of Green Porcelain
sections.summary:
The distant palace proves to be a ruined museum. The traveler searches its broken displays and finds a bar of iron, matches, and materials that can help him make fire. Relics of earlier knowledge are useful even though their institution has collapsed.

He and Weena leave before night, carrying the few objects that might let them reach the sphinx. The museum shows a future littered with the remains of human achievement but unable to preserve the understanding behind it.

sections.label: Chapter XII
sections.title: In the Darkness
sections.summary:
The traveler and Weena enter the woods as night falls. Morlocks surround them; he uses fire and his iron bar to resist. The flames spread beyond his control, turning the forest into a dangerous blaze.

By morning he survives, but Weena is gone. He cannot rescue her and must continue alone. The chapter makes the cost of his struggle concrete: even the tools that protect him can create a disaster he cannot reverse.

sections.label: Chapter XIII
sections.title: The Trap of the White Sphinx
sections.summary:
Back at the sphinx, the traveler finds its pedestal open and his machine inside. He understands that the Morlocks have set a trap. He enters anyway, fights off their grasping hands, and restores the machine’s controls in time to escape.

The contest is brief but decisive. Having learned to distrust the future’s calm appearance, he survives by acting on the evidence before him rather than on his earlier hopeful theory.

sections.label: Chapter XIV
sections.title: The Further Vision
sections.summary:
Instead of stopping in his own century, the traveler moves much farther forward. He sees an enormous red sun, a bleak shore, and strange creatures beneath a dying sky. Human societies and their conflicts have vanished from view.

The journey becomes a vision of planetary time rather than social change. Frightened and weakened, he turns the machine back, carrying an experience far larger than the original dinner-table argument about the fourth dimension.

sections.label: Chapter XV
sections.title: The Time Traveller’s Return
sections.summary:
The traveler reaches his laboratory and finds the familiar world almost unchanged. He is exhausted, and the machine bears signs of its journey. His return brings the narrative back to the dinner guests who have been waiting for an explanation.

He finishes the story after eating and recovering enough to speak. The ordinary room now seems strange to him, while his listeners must decide what weight to give an account they cannot independently verify.

sections.label: Chapter XVI
sections.title: After the Story
sections.summary:
The guests debate the traveler’s account, and the narrator considers the flowers he brought from the future. The Time Traveller soon sets out again, promising to return with further proof, but he disappears and does not come back.

The frame story ends without a final demonstration. What remains is the narrator’s uncertainty and the possibility that the flowers, however small, are evidence of a world no one else has seen.

102.deck: Four friends find adventure, trouble, and a durable home along the river.
overview: Mole discovers the River Bank through Rat, while Toad’s enthusiasms repeatedly put everyone at risk.
The book moves between comic mishaps and quieter moments of belonging, friendship, and wonder.
takeaways: Rat, Mole, Badger, and Toad show different ways of caring for a place and one another.
Toad’s adventures are funny because his confidence so often outruns his judgment.
Home is both a place to return to and a relationship sustained by friends.

sections.label: Chapter I
sections.title: The River Bank
sections.summary:
Mole abandons his spring cleaning and emerges into the sunlight. He meets Water Rat, who takes him boating and introduces him to the rhythms and pleasures of the river. Mole’s curiosity makes an ordinary day feel like the beginning of a new life.

Rat teaches him to row, feeds him, and welcomes him into a world of small rituals. Their friendship begins without a grand quest; the river itself supplies enough discovery for Mole to want to stay.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: The Open Road
sections.summary:
Rat and Mole visit the wealthy, restless Toad, who has become obsessed with a horse-drawn caravan. He persuades them to travel with him, but a passing motor-car wrecks the caravan and immediately captures Toad’s attention.

Toad abandons one passion for another. Rat sees how dangerous this new enthusiasm may become, while Toad orders a costly motor-car as soon as he can. The journey teaches the friends less about the road than about Toad’s impulsiveness.

sections.label: Chapter III
sections.title: The Wild Wood
sections.summary:
Mole ventures alone into the Wild Wood hoping to meet Badger. As night falls, the trees and watching eyes frighten him, and he loses his way in the snow. Rat comes searching and refuses to leave him behind.

The two find shelter at Badger’s door. Mole’s adventure strips away the easy confidence of the river, while Rat’s rescue shows how friendship works when curiosity becomes danger. The shift from the familiar river to the woods makes Mole’s curiosity feel suddenly dangerous.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: Mr. Badger
sections.summary:
Badger takes Mole and Rat in, gives them food and warmth, and hears about Toad’s motor-car trouble. He promises to help curb Toad’s reckless habits. The Wild Wood, frightening from outside, contains a home built on steadiness and care.

Badger also tells Mole about the people who once occupied the land and left it behind. His account places the animals’ lives within a longer history and makes their familiar paths feel both secure and changeable.

sections.label: Chapter V
sections.title: Dulce Domum
sections.summary:
On the way home, Mole catches the scent of his own old burrow and becomes overwhelmed by longing. Rat recognizes the feeling and turns back with him. The little house is dusty and bare after Mole’s absence, but the friends make it welcoming again.

They prepare a meal and greet young field mice who come caroling outside. Mole’s return does not cancel his new river life; it lets him see that an old home and a new friendship can both belong to him.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: Mr. Toad
sections.summary:
Badger, Rat, and Mole confront Toad about his reckless driving and try to keep him at Toad Hall. Toad escapes their watch, takes another motor-car without permission, and is arrested after a wild ride.

His charm and confidence cannot talk him out of the consequences. The court sends him to prison, ending one kind of freedom and setting up an even more elaborate series of escapes. Toad’s friends hope the shock will interrupt a habit he keeps mistaking for freedom.

sections.label: Chapter VII
sections.title: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
sections.summary:
Rat and Mole search the river at night for Portly, the otter’s missing child. Their journey leads them to a quiet island where they glimpse a mysterious, protective presence and find Portly safe.

The chapter pauses the comedy to make the river feel sacred and strange. As morning comes, the animals keep the feeling of the encounter even though its details begin to fade. The chapter pauses the larger adventures for an encounter that the animals struggle to describe.

sections.label: Chapter VIII
sections.title: Toad’s Adventures
sections.summary:
In prison, Toad wins the sympathy of a jailer’s daughter and escapes disguised as a washerwoman. He makes his way onto a train, narrowly evades pursuit, and finds himself free but hungry and far from home.

The disguise works only while Toad can keep his pride quiet. His escape depends on the help of others and on quick improvisation, qualities he will need again before he reaches the river. His confidence returns as soon as he sees a chance to regain the wheel.

sections.label: Chapter IX
sections.title: Wayfarers All
sections.summary:
Rat listens to a migrating sea rat and becomes captivated by distant ports and a life of constant travel. For a time the pull of the open world nearly overcomes his attachment to the river bank.

Mole sees his friend’s distress and gently brings him back to his own home and work. The episode gives Rat a temptation as powerful as Toad’s, but quieter: the desire to leave a beloved place for every place he has not seen.

sections.label: Chapter X
sections.title: The Further Adventures of Toad
sections.summary:
Toad’s journey home continues through mishaps on a barge, a stolen horse, and another encounter with a motor-car. He is repeatedly rescued by luck and then undone by his own boasting.

At last he reaches the river and finds Rat. The adventures have not yet made Toad humble, but they have brought him close enough to hear what has happened to his home in his absence. Even after his escape, his pride keeps turning simple travel into another risky performance.

sections.label: Chapter XI
sections.title: Like Summer Tempests Came His Tears
sections.summary:
Rat tells Toad that stoats and weasels have taken over Toad Hall. Toad’s outrage soon gives way to despair, and Badger and Mole return with a plan to enter through a secret passage.

The friends prepare carefully, while Toad keeps imagining himself the hero of the story. Reclaiming the house will require him to follow other people’s judgment rather than rush toward another performance. Toad’s return brings the story back to the home and friendships his adventures disrupted.

sections.label: Chapter XII
sections.title: The Return of Ulysses
sections.summary:
Badger leads Rat, Mole, and Toad through the passage into Toad Hall. They surprise the occupiers and drive them out. A feast follows, but the friends insist that Toad speak modestly and recognize their help.

Toad tries to restrain his vanity, at least for the moment. The book ends with the friends together in a restored home, balancing the pleasures of adventure with the steadier work of belonging. The ending restores everyday life beside the river after the disorder of Toad’s escapades.

103.deck: An American family treats an English haunting as a household inconvenience—until one daughter listens.
overview: The Otis family buys Canterville Chase despite warnings about its ghost.
Their practical jokes defeat his theatrical scares, but Virginia discovers a sorrow the others have missed.
takeaways: The story uses the family’s pragmatism to satirize old ghost-story conventions.
Virginia’s compassion succeeds where ridicule and fear do not.
The ghost’s release gives the comedy an unexpectedly gentle ending.

sections.label: Chapter I
sections.title: A haunted purchase
sections.summary:
American minister Hiram Otis buys Canterville Chase even after Lord Canterville warns him that the house is haunted. The Otis family arrives and meets the housekeeper, who shows them an old bloodstain in the library.

Rather than accept the stain as a fearful sign, the family sets about cleaning it. Their matter-of-fact response unsettles the expected rules of a ghost story before the ghost himself appears. The opening places the American family’s practical confidence against the house’s much older traditions.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: The ghost meets the family
sections.summary:
The bloodstain returns in new colors, frustrating the family’s attempts to remove it. When the ghost rattles his chains at night, Mr. Otis offers him oil to stop the noise. The twins answer his scares with practical tricks of their own.

For the ghost, centuries of successful haunting are suddenly useless. He feels insulted that his performance is treated as a nuisance rather than a terror and begins planning a more impressive revenge.

sections.label: Chapter III
sections.title: A failed campaign
sections.summary:
The ghost prepares elaborate appearances, but the family repeatedly defeats or ignores them. A false ghost built by the twins frightens him in turn. The legend of Canterville Chase has met a household that refuses to play its assigned part.

His anger becomes mixed with embarrassment and fear. What had seemed a simple contest between a ghost and new owners starts to expose how isolated the ghost has become in his own home.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: The exhausted performer
sections.summary:
Weeks of failed scares leave the ghost weak and miserable. He tries new disguises, but the twins continue to make the corridors dangerous for him. Even a planned appearance before a visiting duke is abandoned when the ghost cannot face another humiliation.

The comic reversals become more pointed as his confidence collapses. He has a long history of frightening others, yet now cannot sleep peacefully or carry out the role by which he understands himself.

sections.label: Chapter V
sections.title: Virginia listens
sections.summary:
Virginia finds the ghost alone and speaks to him without mockery. He tells her of his weariness and of a prophecy that may allow him to rest. She chooses to help, even though the path he shows her is frightening.

The hidden doorway closes behind them. Where her family tried cleaning, oil, and tricks, Virginia offers attention to a person whose suffering has been obscured by his theatrical reputation. Virginia’s willingness to listen gives the ghost something the family’s jokes and cleaning products could not.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: The hidden chamber
sections.summary:
Virginia disappears, and the family searches the house in growing alarm. She returns after passing through the ghost’s secret realm, carrying a box of jewels and leading them to a chamber with his remains.

She explains that she prayed for him and helped him find peace. Her return changes the family’s understanding of the haunting: the ghost’s freedom depended on compassion, not on defeating him. The family’s alarm also reveals that Virginia’s compassion has carried a real cost for her.

sections.label: Chapter VII
sections.title: A quiet ending
sections.summary:
The family gives the ghost a funeral, and Canterville Chase is finally at rest. Virginia later marries the young duke who had cared for her, but she keeps the details of her encounter with the ghost private.

The closing conversation suggests that the experience taught her something about life, death, and love that she cannot fully put into words. The farce ends with a mystery treated respectfully rather than explained away.
